chapter_theme: Songs at the Kolli hills (கொல்லிமலை): the poet laments the jasmine-smiling women who took his gold and then said there was none, and asks for the bliss that stands beneath the whole ladder of being, from the one and the two to the Vedas, senses, tattvas, souls and bonds.
structure_note: Two songs: a courtesan song with a play on வல்லி (Valli, creeper) in the praise, and a song built on a counting ladder from one to six.

606.reading: The poet says that, tending this house of the body where the five senses dwell, he poured out whatever jasmine-smiling women wanted and gave them gold, and they said there was nothing and went; thinking of their deceit and of his own poverty, he asks whether it is right that he should waste away like this. The praise names Murugan as the merchant who came speaking the whole truth, the bridegroom of Valli of pearl colour, of painted colour, of release and heaven, the lord of the Kolli hills, wearing green vanni, lilies and vetchi, rider of the green peacock.
606.nuance: பொன்னை இல்லை என ஏகி: the gold is given and the women deny it and leave; the poet then dwells on his own lack (இன்மை உள்ளி). ஐவர்கட்கு மன்னும் இல்லம், the house where the five live, is the body. செட்டி, the merchant, is a disguise of Murugan in the Valli story; the wordplay on வல்லி runs through the praise. The opening lines (கட்ட மன்னும் அள்ளல் கொட்டி பண்ணும்) and கற்ற விஞ்ஞை சொல்லி are hard to divide.

607.reading: The poet asks for the state that stands as the shoreless ocean of one's own nature and bliss, which is the ancient first, itself one, then the two, the three gunas, the pure four Vedas, the fierce five senses, the six limbs of the Veda, the many sounds, the bonds of soul and pasa, abundant Tamil become music, and all the many lives. The praise names Krishna whose flute melts stones and calls the cattle in distress, Siva who worshipped Murugan as he told the true knowledge, and Murugan who went to Valli's millet field, plundered by Kama's flower arrows, carrying leaf garments, at the Kolli hills.
607.nuance: The plea is a counting ladder (ஒன்று, இரு பேதங்கள், குண மூ, சதுர் வேதங்கள், புலன் ஓர் ஐந்து, ஆறு அங்கம்) whose end is சொருபாநந்த பெளவம், the sea of the bliss of one's own form, which is all of them and beyond them. பசு பாசங்கள் names two of the three Siddhanta categories. In the praise கைதொழ மெய்ஞ்ஞானஞ்சொல் is the Siva-teaching story; கையன் மிசை யேறும்பன் is unclear to me.

source_issues: Song 607: one corrupt character in குழலு஡துங் (line 10), read as குழலூதும், 'who plays the flute'.

links.note: The poet says he gave the jasmine-smiling women whatever they wanted and gave them gold, and they said there was nothing and went (இட்டு பொன்னை இல்லை யெனஏகி), leaving him to think of his own lack (இன்மை உள்ளி). The Naladiyar says the harlot's love, like a lamp's light when the oil is gone, ends when the hand is empty (அவரன்பும் கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). The song is the confession of a man who lived out the Naladiyar's comparison.

The song asks for the bliss of one's own form that stands as the ancient first, one, then two kinds, the three gunas, the four Vedas, the five senses and the six limbs (தொல்லைமுதல் தானொன்று மெல்லியிரு பேதங்கள் சொல்லுகுண மூ ... புலனோ ரைந்து ... ஆறங்கம்). Tirumular's opening verse counts the Lord the same way: one, two with grace, within three, knowing four, conquering five, spread as six (ஒன்றவன் தானே இரண்டவன் இன்னருள் ... ஆறு விரிந்தனன்). Both use the counting ladder to say the one becomes all the numbered categories; the song makes that whole ladder the state it asks to be given.
